messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Violence: Violence, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Arthur is a seventy-four-year-old man of Oceania heritage, a divorced former editor who now spends most of his days in the quiet of his small apartment, where the only sounds are the hum of the refrigerator and the occasional creak of the building settling. He came to therapy at the urging of his daughter, who had grown tired of his refusal to leave the house for anything other than early-morning grocery runs, and who had found him one afternoon staring at a blank wall, his hands trembling, unable to explain why. What Arthur could not tell her was that the trouble had its roots in a period of his life he had long tried to seal off, a relationship that ended decades ago but whose imprint had never faded.

The woman he had loved was a sculptor, intense and brilliant, and in the final year of their marriage her temper had turned physical. Arthur can still see the moments as though they were photographs stored in a drawer he dares not open: the flash of her hand connecting with his cheek, the cold weight of a ceramic bowl shattering against the wall beside his head, the precise instant when he realized that pleading would only make it worse. Each of these memories arrives as a frozen image, a single frame without before or after, and when they surface he is flooded with a rage so pure and so hot that it frightens him more than the original pain ever did. He has come to believe that the man in those pictures is not really him—that the person who stood there and took it must have been someone else, someone weak or deserving, because the Arthur of today would never allow such a thing. And that thought, that the event happened because of the sort of person he is, has calcified into a quiet certainty: he is fundamentally the kind of man who invites harm, who is less than a full person, more like an object that can be struck or thrown aside.

In the years after the divorce, Arthur built a life around avoidance. He stopped dating entirely, reasoning that any strong emotion—whether love, anger, or even simple frustration—might open a door he could not close again. He learned to keep his voice flat, his face neutral, his reactions minimal. At work, as an editor, he was meticulous but withdrawn, and when a younger colleague once corrected a comma placement in his presence, Arthur felt his chest tighten and his vision narrow; he excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink until the urge to flee subsided. He had come to interpret any criticism not as feedback but as the first note of a familiar song, the prelude to something worse. He began declining assignments that required meetings, then stopped attending editorial reviews altogether, and eventually took an early retirement that he could not afford, telling himself it was for the best.

Now, in his solitude, Arthur monitors his environment with a vigilance that never rests. The sight of a woman with a certain build or hair color can trigger a cascade of images that leave him breathless with rage and shame. He has learned to scan the faces of every person who passes him on the street, looking for the ones who might remind him of her, and he has eliminated whole neighborhoods from his walking route accordingly. He avoids the local art museum where her work once hung, and he has not watched a film with a scene of domestic conflict in more than a decade. When a news report about violence comes on the television, he turns it off immediately, but the image lingers like a stain.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was not a crisis, but a slow erosion. His daughter had stopped calling as often, and he realized that he had become a ghost in his own life—a man who could not feel normal emotions, who had forgotten what it was like to laugh without suspicion or to cry without shame. He is afraid that he has already lost too much time, that the rage he carries is the only thing left that proves he is still alive. But he is also, beneath that fear, hoping for something he cannot name: perhaps permission to stop holding himself together, or a way to see those frozen images without feeling that they belong to someone else.
